2.88.m:
Kuñjala said:
The vow, the hymn, the great knowledge, and the meditation of Viṣṇu
which destroys sin have been declared by me before you, O good son.

When that virtuous woman performs this fourfold practice,
she goes to the realm of Viṣṇu, difficult even for the gods to attain.

Go from here, dear child, and awaken the celestial lady;
declare to her the king of vows called Aśūnyaśayana.

Deliver the illustrious princess from her great sin.
What was asked by you has been declared by me, bestowing merit and destroying sin.

Go, go, O fortunate one!" Having spoken thus, he ceased.
Glorious Viṣṇu said:
When Ujjvala was thus spoken to by his father Kuñjala,

the righteous and wise Ujjvala bowed to the feet
of his parents and went swiftly, O king, to Plakṣadvīpa,

to that mountain auspicious on all sides, filled with various minerals,
adorned with lofty peaks consisting of various gems,

with waters shining and full of various streams, O king;
there are rivers of clear water on that best of excellent mountains.

There Kinnaras sing, and Gandharvas with melodious voices, O king;
it is crowded with Apsarases and frequented by hosts of gods,

resounded by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, adorned by hosts of sages,
and filled everywhere with the cries of various birds.

Thus reaching the mountain, Ujjvala of swift stride
[saw] that maiden weeping bitterly on that mountain.

The wise one spoke these words to her who was weeping profusely:
"Who are you, O blessed one? Why do you weep now?

To whom do you belong, O fortunate lady? By whom was an offense done to you?
Tell me today the cause of all your grief."

Who are you, O fortunate one, afflicted out of compassion for me?
Bearing the form of a bird, dear child, you speak joyfully."

Hearing all that which was spoken by the princess:
"I am a bird, O fortunate lady, afflicted out of compassion for you.
I have taken the form of a bird, gentle lady; I am not an adept, nor am I wise. / I saw you here weeping with great lamentations.
Therefore I ask you, O lady: tell me the cause here, / what happened in your father's house, your own history indeed."
She reported everything in order, causing sorrow. / Having heard it in brief, the noble-minded Ujjvala,
the great bird, spoke to her, the very sorrowful divine lady: / "How at the time of marriage your husbands met their death,
and the kṣatriyas went to destruction on account of your svayaṃvara— / all this conduct of yours was related by me to my father.
Your sinful deed performed in another birth, O fair-eyed one, / was out of compassion related by my father before me.
You were nourished and tainted by that fault, O woman of lovely face; / all this reason was related by my father.
Experience the fruition of past karma and take heart." / Having thus heard that speech of Ujjvala, the maiden,
bowing down with plaintive words, spoke back to that noble bird: / "O bird, show mercy to me!
Tell me by your grace the expiation for that sin, / and the most auspicious atonement that purifies my transgression,
by which I may attain merit, purified and cleansed of defilement. / O fortunate one, tell me the atonement out of your grace!"
Ujjvala said: / "For your sake, O fortunate lady, I asked my father; / an unexcelled atonement was therefore declared by my father.
Perform that, O fortunate lady, which cleanses all transgression: / Meditate indeed on Hṛṣīkeśa and repeat his hundred names.
Ever devoted to knowledge of the truth, observe the unexcelled vow, / the meritorious Aśūnyaśayana vow that destroys sin."
That righteous bird explained what illuminates all knowledge— / the knowledge, the hymn of praise, the vow, and the meditation of the great-souled Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu said: / “Therefore she indeed set out and lived in a desolate forest; / freed from all dualities, she became established in ascetic austerity.”
Having conquered her food, without support, deeply sorrowful, / devoid of desire and anger, constantly restraining her senses,
and casting away great delusion, O great king, she observed the vow. / When the fourth year arrived, Janārdana was well pleased.
Desiring to grant her a boon, the lord of boons came; / the boon-granting Lord showed her his own form.
Sūta said: / [She saw] the great Lord, dark as a cloud of sapphire, holding the conch, discus, and mace, / rich in the splendor of all ornaments, with a lotus in his hand.
Folding her hands in reverence, trembling and without shelter, / bowing down, she spoke to Madhusūdana in faltering words:
"By your divine radiance I am indeed unable to stand. / Who are you of divine form that has appeared out of compassion before me?
Tell me by your grace: what is your purpose here? / Tell me everything out of grace, O high-minded one.
I recognize that you are a god by your radiance and gestures; / bereft of knowledge, O Lord of the World, I know neither your form nor your name.
Are you Brahmā, or are you Viṣṇu, or are you indeed Śaṃkara?" / Having spoken thus and bowed down, she fell like a rod to the earth.
The Lord of the World spoke to that princess who was bowed down. / The Holy Lord said: / "There is no difference among the three gods, O fair one.
He by whom Brahmā is worshipped, or Śaṃkara, O woman of lovely face— / by him I am constantly worshipped; no doubt should be entertained here.
These two are not different from me, and I am ever possessed of three forms. / By those by whom I am worshipped, those two are also well worshipped.
I am the god Hṛṣīkeśa, come to you out of compassion. / Through this meritorious praise, vow, and observance,
you have become free from defilements; choose a boon, O fair lady!" / The divine lady said: / "Triumph, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Kṛṣṇa, dispeller of distress!
“I bow to your two feet; deliver me, O lord of the gods! / If you desire to grant me a boon, O bearer of the discus, be gracious to me.”
Give me devotion to your two feet, O sinless one; / show me, O Lord of the World, the path of liberation free from disease.
Grant servitude to you, O Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, if you are pleased, O Janārdana!" / The Holy Lord said: / "So be it, O fortunate lady; go, with your defilements shaken off,
to the supreme realm of Viṣṇu, which is ever difficult even for yogins to attain. / Go, go to the supreme realm now by my grace!"
When that speech had been spoken by the noble Mādhava, / the divine lady became celestial, with a radiance equal to the splendor of the sun.
As all the worlds looked on, adorned with celestial ornaments, / provided with celestial garlands and hanging with celestial necklaces,
she went to the realm of Viṣṇu, devoid of conflagration and dissolution. / The bird returned again to his home filled with joy.
That most virtuous one related all that to his father.

2.89.m: Viṣṇu said: / Then Kuñjala spoke these words to his son Samujjvala: / "Tell me, O son, what unprecedented thing did you see?
Tell that to me gladly; I am now eager to hear." / Having thus instructed that son, Kuñjala fell silent.
Then the son, bowed down with humility, replied to his father. / Samujjvala said: / "To Himavant, the best of mountains, accompanied by hosts of gods,
I go for the sake of food for yourself and for myself, O father. / There I see a wonder not seen nor heard of before:
a region crowded with hosts of sages, adorned with apsarases, / rich in the beauty of many wonders, auspicious and endowed with blessings,
then with various forests endowed with many meritorious fruits, / captivating the mind with an abundance of many wonders.
There was seen by me, O father, an unprecedented thing near Mānasa: / along with many swans came a single swan.
Thus other black ones arrived there, O fortunate one, / with beaks and feet of different colors, but elsewhere with white bodies.
Such ones were blue indeed, and others white, O wise one. / Four women were also there, of terrible appearance and terrifying,
cruel with formidable fangs, frightful with their hair standing erect. / Afterward, they arrived at that Mānasa lake.
The black swans bathed in Mānasa before my eyes, O father; / they wandered all around, and the others did not bathe there in Mānasa.
Those women laughed, O father, with harsh, loud laughter. / Out of that lake emerged a single large-bodied swan.
Afterward three emerged, and I was disregarded by them; / disputing with one another, they departed through the sky.
Those terribly terrifying women wandered about on all sides. / On an auspicious peak of the Vindhya, in the shade of the trees, the birds
sat there, all of them consumed by severe grief. / As they were watching closely, a Bhilla arrived,
who had tormented deer, carrying arrows in his hand and holding a bow; / resorting to a rocky slab, he sat down in comfort.
Afterwards, the Bhilla woman arrived, bringing food and water. / O king, she looked upon her beloved who was endowed with joyful signs,
and seeing her lover transformed, surrounded with splendor, / overcome by divine radiance like the sun standing in the sky,
believing him to be another man, she abandoned him and was about to go. / The hunter said: “Come, come here, my beloved! Why do you not look at me?
I am afflicted with hunger, and I am watching for you.” / Hearing his words, the hunter woman quickly approached.
Approaching her husband's side, she was then filled with wonder: / “What kind of radiant appearance is this? Which god is calling me?”
Then the hunter woman spoke to her husband of blazing radiance: / “What did you do here, brave one? Who are you, endowed with divine signs?”
Sūta said: / Addressed in this way by the hunter woman, the hunter spoke to his beloved: / “I am your husband, my lovely one, and you are my beloved wife.
Why do you not recognize me? Why does doubt arise? / Afflicted with hunger, I am awaiting water and food.”
The hunter woman said: / “Rude, black-complexioned, red-eyed, wearing a black garment— / such is my husband, terrifying to all living beings.
Who are you with a divine body, who calls out saying ‘beloved’? / This doubt has arisen in me; speak the truth before me.”
He told in detail to his beloved his lineage, name, his own village, his pastime, bodily mark, his son and daughter, / in order to convince her.
With a delighted mind, that hunter woman replied to her husband: / “Why has your body become like this, wearing white garments?
Tell me how it came to be; wonder has arisen in me.” / Thus being questioned by his wife, the deer-slayer—
Sūta said: / —having heard that beloved who was filled with modesty, then replied: / “O lady of good vows, there is a confluence on the northern bank of the Narmadā.
My spirit had become exceedingly distressed by the heat, O dear one. / Exhausted by fatigue, I quickly went to this very confluence, my lovely one,
bathed, drank water, and then came back. / Ever since then, my body has become thus, covered with radiance,
provided with garments, and my jacket has attained whiteness.” / By those previously mentioned bodily marks, lineage, and dwelling place,
she recognized her beloved and, realizing the occurrence of merit, / then answered her husband: “Show me the confluence.
Afterward, I will give you food along with drink.” / Thus spoken to by his beloved, the hunter went quickly.
The sin-destroying confluence was then shown by him ahead. / O highly fortunate one, the birds, of swift flight, having flown up,
all went along with her to that excellent confluence on the Revā. / As those birds were watching and as I was looking on,
her husband was bathed by her, and she herself also bathed. / Both became bearers of divine bodies, endowed with divine splendor,
O best of birds, adorned with divine garments and ointments, / wearing divine garlands and robes, anointed with divine fragrant perfumes.
Having mounted a Vaiṣṇava vehicle, honored by sages and gandharvas, / worshipped by Vaiṣṇavas, the two went to the world of Viṣṇu.
I saw those two noble-souled spouses being praised, / proceeding along the heavenly path, and the birds chirped likewise.
Then, having seen the supreme king of sacred places, with words expressing joy, / four black geese [plunged] into that sin-destroying confluence;
having bathed and purified by their intent, they regained brightness. / Having bathed and drunk water, they came out again.
Just as many black women died simply from that bath. / Crying out, trembling, shaking with cries of woe,
they went to the world of Yama, seen by me at that time, O father. / Then those geese, having flown up, went toward their own place.
Thus, O father, what was witnessed directly by me has been told to you: / those huge-bodied geese with black wings and those women.
Explain by your grace, O father: who will they become? / Tell me about the geese that came forth from the midst of the Mānasa lake;
who will they become, O father? Explain that now. / Why did the geese become very black, and become purified again
at that very moment, O father, and why did those women die? / Thus, O father, a dreadful doubt has arisen in my heart.
You ought to cut it away this very day, as you are skilled in knowledge, / having your face turned kindly in grace towards me who am ever bowed before you.”
Having addressed his father in this manner, Samujjvala fell silent. / Then that parrot named Kuñjala began to speak.

2.90.m: Sūta said: / Having heard all that speech of Samujjvala, / that righteous-minded Kuñjala replied to his son.
Kuñjala said: / “I shall tell it, O father; let it be heard with a steady mind— / this sin-destroying account which wipes away all doubts.
In the world of Indra, a delightful dialogue concerning the gods took place / in the assembly of that deity, the great-souled Indra.
Nārada went swiftly to see the thousand-eyed god. / The thousand-eyed one, seeing him arrived,
shining with luster equal to the sun's splendor, was filled with joy; rising, the wise one / gave water for honoring and foot-washing, with his mind bowed down in devotion.
Having joined his palms, he then made an obeisance; / seating the best of the twice-born on a soft, sacred seat,
bowing down, endowed with supreme faith, he asked: / ‘Why is your arrival today? Tell me the reason now.’
Thus addressed by the king of the gods, the great sage replied: / “Purandara has indeed come to earth to see you.”
having bathed with deep faith in sacred regions and tīrthas, / having worshipped the gods and ancestors, having seen numerous tīrthas.
All this has been related to you as was previously asked by you.’ / Devendra said: ‘Holy tīrthas and auspicious fields were seen by you, O sage;
by reaching which tīrtha is a slayer of a brahmin freed from the murder of a brahmin, / a drinker of liquor freed from sin, a cow-killer, or a stealer of gold?
How can one who betrays his master or one who slays a woman be happy, O highly fortunate one?’ / Nārada said: ‘Whichever tīrthas there are, Gayā and the rest, O lord of gods,
I do not know any specific sin-destroying distinction among them. / They are very holy, very divine, sin-destroying, and equal.
I know all the excellent tīrthas, O Purandara; / difference or non-difference I do not know at present.
Let a test be made, O god, regarding the tīrthas which grant liberation.’ / Hearing those words of the noble Nārada,
the tīrthas existing on earth were summoned by Indra. / Divine, embodied forms arrived by his command,
with joined hands, divine, decorated with fine ornaments, / wearing divine garments, gentle, and radiant, O one of good vows,
formed especially in the likeness of women and men, / resembling gold and sandalwood, and bearing divine forms.”
With the color of a pearl they shine, O lord of men; / some have the hue of heated gold, and others are reddish indeed.
Some, white and bright yellow, shine within the assembly; / some resemble lotuses—these having taken physical form.
Having the brilliance of the sun, and resembling the radiance of lightning, / and others shining like fire, they blaze within the assembly.
Rich with the splendor of every ornament, they shine, O lord of men, / with necklaces, bracelets, armlets, garlands, and fine sandal paste.
Anointed with heavenly sandalwood, fragrant and grand, / holding water pots in their hands, they arrived inside the assembly.
The Gaṅgā, the sacred Narmadā, Candrabhāgā, Sarasvatī, / Devikā, Bimbikā, Kubjā, Kuñjalā, the famed Mañjulā,
Rambhā, the sacred Bhānumatī, Pārā, and the fair Ghargharā, / Śoṇā, Sindhu-Sauvīrā, Kāverī, and Kapilā,
Kumudā, the sacred Vedanadī, the most holy Maheśvarī, / the famed Carmaṇvatī, Lopā, and the fair Kauśikī,
Suhamsī, Haṃsapādā, Haṃsavegā, Manorathā, / Suruthā, Svāruṇā, Veṇā, Bhadraveṇā, fair Padminī,
Nāhalī, the other Sumarīcā, and the holy Pulidikā, / Hemā, the celestial Manorathā, Candrikā, Vedasaṅkramā,
Jvālā, Hutāśanī, Svāhā, Kālā, and Kapiñjalā, / Svadhā, fair Kalāliṅgā, Gambhīrā, Bhīmavāhinī,
Devadrīcī, Vīravāhā, Lakṣahomā, Aghāpahā, / Pārāśarī, Hemagarbhā, Subhadrā, Vasuputrikā—
these rivers, exceedingly holy, personified, O lord of men, / rich with the splendor of all ornaments, holding jars in their hands, well honored.
Prayāga, Puṣkara, Arghadīrgha, Manorathā, / most sacred Vārāṇasī, remover of the killing of a brahmin,
Dvārāvatī, Prabhāsa, Avantī, Naimiṣa as well, / Caṇḍaka, Mahāratna, Maheśvara and Kaleśvara,
Kalijara, Brahmakṣetra, Māthura, Mānavāhaka, / Māyā, Kāntī, and other celestial and diverse [sacred places],
the sixty-eight holy pilgrimage sites, and the hundred crores of rivers / led by the Godāvarī, all arrived at his command.
All the great holy pilgrimage sites of the continents, / assuming personified forms, [came] to the thousand-eyed lord of the gods.
All of them assembled, executing his command, / and bowed to the lord of the gods with bowed heads on every side.
Sūta said: / The glorious king of the gods was addressed by those great pilgrimage sites: / “Why have we been summoned by you, O god of gods? Tell us!
Tell us the entire reason; homage to you, O ruler of the gods!” / Having heard that statement of theirs, the king of the gods spoke:
“Which great pilgrimage site is capable of removing the killing of a brahmin, / the great sin called cow-killing, and the unsurpassed [sin] called woman-killing,
that born of betrayal of one's master, and the terrible [sin] of drinking liquor, / that arising from the theft of gold, and that produced by reviling the guru?
Who is capable of destroying the most dreadful killing of an embryo, / the great sin arising from treason against the king, which causes much suffering,
and that from betrayal of a friend, and another, breach of trust, / then division of the gods, and beyond that, division of the liṅga,
the cutting off of the livelihood of brahmins, destruction of cow pastures, / the burning down of a sanctuary, and the setting fire to a house?
These sixteen are the great sins; and incestuous intercourse, / that arising from abandonment of one's master, or from fleeing the battlefield—
who indeed is able to destroy these, being the foremost pilgrimage site? / Who among you is truly capable, without expiation?
While the deities look on, and while Nārada looks on, / let all of you deliberate, reflect, and state with absolute certainty.”
When this auspicious speech had been spoken by the high-souled king of the gods, / having consulted together with the king of pilgrimage sites, they addressed Śakra present in the assembly.
The pilgrimage sites said: / “May it be heard! We shall declare it, O king of the gods; homage to you! / Truly, all pilgrimage sites exist, and they remove all sins.
Yet the killing of a brahmin and the others mentioned by you, O lord of the gods, / most terrible and blazing, we are simply unable to destroy.
Prayāga, Puṣkara, the unsurpassed Arghatīrtha, / and fortunate Vārāṇasī are capable of destroying sin.
For the purpose of destroying the great sins, these four possess boundless valor; / for the purpose of destroying the secondary sins, these four possess boundless valor.
They were created by the Creator, O lord of the gods, led by Puṣkara, endowed with great strength.” / Having thus heard that speech of the pilgrimage sites, the king of gods then,
seized with great joy, made a hymn of praise to them.

2.91.m: Kuñjala said: / When formerly the thousand-eyed one was overwhelmed by the killing of a brahmin, / through union with the beloved of Gautama, the great [sin of] incestuous intercourse,
sin arose in him, and he was abandoned by gods and brahmins. / The thousand-eyed one performed austerities, without support, without refuge.
At the conclusion of the austerities, all the deities, ṛṣis, yakṣas, and kinnaras / performed an abhiseka for the worship of the king of the gods.
Having brought the king of the gods to the region of Mālava, O best of sons, / [he] performed the bath, O highly fortunate one, with jars filled with water.
He was first taken by himself to be bathed at Vārāṇasī; / then at Prayāga, O thousand-eyed one, and then again at Arghatīrtha;
at Puṣkara that great-souled one was bathed by himself indeed / by all the gods headed by Brahmā and multitudes of sages, O best of the twice-born;
by nāgas, trees, serpents, gandharvas, and kinnaras; / and the king of the gods was bathed, properly consecrated with Vedic mantras
by the sages who destroy all sins at that time, O best of the twice-born. / When that fortunate, high-souled thousand-eyed one was purified,
the killing of a brahmin left him, and the incestuous intercourse likewise. / Then the killing of a brahmin was destroyed along with the incestuous intercourse,
together with that terrible sin of Indra on the surface of the earth. / The thousand-eyed one, highly pleased, granted a boon to the pilgrimage sites:
“You shall be the kings of pilgrimage sites, without a doubt, / and holy by my grace, since I have been freed
from this most terrible transgression by you who are immaculate.” / Having thus granted a boon to them, he granted a boon to Mālava:
“Since my impurity, which brought fatigue, was held by you today, / therefore you shall be adorned with food and drink, and with wealth and grains.
You will be so, without doubt, by my grace, there is no hesitation; / free from severe times of distress, you will be full of great merit.”
Having thus granted a boon to him, the king of the gods, Puraṃdara, / the sacred fields, all the pilgrimage sites, and the region of Mālava,
they returned to their own abodes together with Indra. / Sūta said: From that time forth, the four—Prayāga, Puṣkara,
Vārāṇasī, and Arghatīrtha—attained supreme kingship [among sacred places].
Kuñjala said: / In the Pañcāla country there was a kṣatriya named Vidura; / formerly, under the influence of delusion, a brahmin was slain by him.
Deprived of topknot and sacred thread, and devoid of sectarian mark, / he wanders about for alms; that slayer of a brahmin has also come here.

"Let alms and food be given to the killer of a Brahmin and drinker of liquor!"
In this way, he formerly wandered and begged among all the houses.

Thus, having wandered through all the sacred pilgrimage sites, he arrived;
yet even so, his guilt of killing a Brahmin did not depart, O best of twice-borns.

Taking shelter in the shade of a tree, his mind burning,
the sinful Vidura remained, overcome with pain and grief.

Then a Brahmin, Candraśarman, afflicted by great delusion,
who lived in the Magadha country and was a killer of his guru,

abandoned by his own people and relatives, wicked-minded,
arrived at that very place where Vidura was staying.

Bereft of topknot and sacred thread, devoid of the marks of a Brahmin,
he was then questioned by the wicked-minded Vidura:

"Who are you that have arrived, unfortunate one with a burning mind?
Devoid of the marks of a Brahmin, why do you wander the earth?"

As soon as he was addressed by Vidura, the lowest of twice-borns, Candraśarman,
recounted everything, just as it had been done by himself before,

and the dreadfully terrifying sin [committed] while living in his guru's house,
fallen into great delusion and overcome with anger:

"The murder of my guru was committed by me previously; by that I am now consumed."
Having recounted the whole story, Candraśarman also asked:

"Who are you, full of extreme sorrow, taking shelter in the shade of a tree?"
Vidura related his own sin in brief.

Then a third twice-born arrived, exhausted by weariness,
named Vedaśarman, bearing an accumulation of many sins.

Questioned thoroughly by the two, "Who are you, looking so sorrowful?
Why do you wander the earth? Speak truly of your condition!"

Vedaśarman then related to them all his own deeds:
indeed, incestuous intercourse with a forbidden woman had been committed [by him].

"Condemned by all people and by other kinsmen and relatives,
defiled by that sin, I thus wander this earth."

Then a Vaiśya named Vamjula arrived, who was a drinker of liquor
and especially a killer of cows; and he was asked by them as before.

By him was declared all the sin that had been committed previously;
everything spoken by him was heard by the others.

In this way, the four most sinful men came together in one place;
no one had any contact with another regarding food or clothing,

O noble one; yet they conversed with one another.
They did not sit on the same seat, nor did they sleep on the same bed.

Thus, overcome with sorrow, they went to various sacred pilgrimage sites;
yet their terrible sins did not perish, O child.

The sacred pilgrimage sites have no power to destroy major sins.
Then Vidura and the others went to Mount Kālañjara.

2.92.m:
Kuñjala said:
Having reached Kālañjara, they dwelt there in extreme sorrow,
consumed by their major sins, crying 'Alas, alas!', devoid of consciousness.

There arrived a certain perfected sage of great renown;
by him they, afflicted with extreme sorrow, were asked: "By what are you distressed?"

He was told by them; very wise and skilled in all knowledge,
learning of their major sins, the richly meritorious one took pity.

The perfected sage said:
"At the conjunction of the new moon and Monday, Prayāga and Puṣkara,
Arghatīrtha as the third, and Vārāṇasī as the fourth—

go there, the four of you fouled by sin;
when you bathe in the water of the Gaṅgā, then you will be liberated

from your sins, there is no doubt; you will attain purity."
Instructed by him, they all bowed to him with devotion.

Then from Kālañjara, afflicted by sin, they quickly departed.
Reaching Vārāṇasī and having bathed, O best of twice-borns,

and [reaching] Prayāga, Puṣkara, and Arghatīrtha, O virtuous one,
having attained that conjunction of the new moon and Monday, they went to that great city.

Vidura, Candraśarman, Vedaśarman as the third,
and the Vaiśya Vamjulaka, a liquor-drinker of sinful mind—

when that sacred day arrived, they bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, O twice-born;
merely by bathing, they were liberated from their sins such as cow-slaughter.

Smeared with sins such as Brahmin-murder, guru-murder, and drinking liquor,
those sacred pilgrimage sites wandered over the earth.

Puṣkara, Ardhatīrtha, Prayāga that destroys sins,
and Vārāṇasī the fourth—these were stained by sins, O best of twice-borns.

They all turned black and wandered in the form of swans;
they bathed in all the excellent sacred pilgrimage sites, O best of twice-borns,

yet the blackness brought upon them by their sins did not depart.
Though they bathed again in all the sacred sites, O great king,

whichever sacred pilgrimage site they went to, all those sacred pilgrimage sites, O best of twice-borns,
went along with them in the form of swans, intensely sorrowful.

Their wives, in the form of their sins, likewise wandered all around;
they wandered in the form of swans to the sixty-eight excellent sacred pilgrimage sites.

Along with them, O great king, together with those great sacred pilgrimage sites,
those men, their minds agitated by sin, came to lake Mānasa.

Though they bathed there, O great king, the sin did not leave them.
With his mind overcome with shame, Mānasa assumed the form of a swan

and became black-bodied, the one whom you saw previously.
Then they went to the northern bank of the Revā, which destroys sin.

At the confluence of the Kubjā, frequented by gods and perfected beings,
merely by bathing they were liberated from their sins, O best of twice-borns.

Casting off that dark color, they attained good merit.
Whichever sacred pilgrimage site they went to, the swans undertook bathing;

those women laughed seeing that the sin was not departing at all.
By the water-fire of the Kubjā, the excellent sin

was reduced to ashes; then those women died—
Brahmin-murder, murder of a guru, liquor-drinking, and incest.

They were turned to ashes, destroyed by the Kubjā of the Revā;
those women, destroyed, O highly fortunate one, died on the riverbank.

They [wandered] to the sixty-eight sacred pilgrimage sites in the form of swans;
know that swan who arrived together with them to be Mānasa.

There were four black swans; hear their names from me:
Prayāga, Puṣkara, the unsurpassed Arghatīrtha,

and Vārāṇasī as the fourth—these four removers of sins,
overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin, wandered about.

These sacred pilgrimage sites, in sorrow, [wandered] among sacred pilgrimage sites, O noble-minded one;
yet as they wandered, O son, that terrible sin did not depart from them.

At the confluence of the Kubjā, they were purified and truly freed from guilt;
for among all holy sacred pilgrimage sites, it is revered here.

Prayāga became the king [of sacred sites] before Indra;
let the sacred pilgrimage sites roar only so long as the Revā is not seen,

which is established for the destruction of sins such as killing a Brahmin.
At the holy confluence of the Kapilā, and likewise at the confluence of the Revā,

at the meeting of the Meghanāda, and likewise at the great confluence,
immensely holy and immensely blessed, the Revā is everywhere difficult to attain.

At Oṃkāra, at Bhṛgukṣetra, and at the confluence of the Narmadā and the Kubjā,
at Māhiṣmatī, the Revā is difficult to be attained by humans and best of gods.
The Revā is holy at the Viṭaṅkā confluence, at Śrīkaṇṭha, and at Maṅgaleśvara; / it is everywhere difficult to reach, filled with the gods' merits.
The mother of sacred fords, the great goddess, the destroyer of masses of sin— / a person is happy anywhere between both its banks.
By a single bath, a human being enjoys the fruit of a horse sacrifice. / All this has been related to you as was questioned by you.
It removes all sins, is holy, and grants [a good] destination to those who hear it." / Having spoken thus, the very wise one addressed his third son.

2.93.m: Kuñjala said: / "What unprecedented thing, full of wonder, was seen by you as you wandered the earth, O Vijvala? / Tell me that, O you of good vows!
Striving to find food, you go to that region from here. / Whatever wondrous thing you have seen, recount it, O best of sons!"
Vijvala said: / "On the ridge of Mount Meru there is a forest named Ānanda, / always filled with divine trees laden with fruits and flowers,
crowded with hosts of gods, accompanied by sages and Siddhas, / by beautiful apsarases, gandharvas, kinnaras, and uragas,
with stepped wells, wells, ponds, and with rivers and streams. / The holy Ānanda forest shines with divine qualities,
resounded with aerial chariots numbering in tens of millions, resembling swans, jasmine, and the moon, / with charming clamors of song, and with the rumbling of clouds.
Everywhere it is sweet with the buzzing of bees, / and surrounded by sandal trees, mango trees, and flowering campakas.
Thus the excellent Ānanda forest shines with various trees, / filled with much tumult from the calls of various birds.
Thus the very beautiful Ānanda [forest] was seen there by me. / And, father, a spotless lake shines there resembling an ocean,
filled with sacred water, with auspicious lotuses and water-lilies, / crowded with aquatic plants, and filled with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks.
Such was the lake right in the middle of that forest, / crowded with gods and gandharvas, and adorned by multitudes of sages.
It shines with kinnaras, uragas, gandharvas, and cāraṇas. / There a wonder was seen by me, father; it cannot be described!
Arriving by a divine aerial chariot, adorned with water-pots, / shining with an umbrella, staff, and banners, O best of beings,
permeated with every enjoyment, sung to by kinnaras, / gandharvas, and apsarases, and shining, O you of good vows,
praised by great Siddhas and ṛṣis who know reality, / matchless in form in the world—such a one was never seen anywhere—
his body adorned with all ornaments, beautified with a divine garland, / with a garland made of great gems shining on his chest.
Standing near him was seen one fair-faced woman / adorned with golden necklaces, pearl armlets, and bracelets,
with divine garments, fragrances, sandalwood, and lovely ointments. / Praised and sung to, the man arrived there.
Shaped like Rati, with lovely hips, plump thighs, and breasts, / her body adorned with all ornaments, she was endowed with such beauty.
Both of them were seen by me having arrived by an aerial chariot, / endowed with beauty, charm, and sweetness, filled with all splendor.
Having descended from the aerial chariot, they came near the lake. / Those noble ones, the man and the woman, lotus-eyed, bathed, O father.
Then, seizing large weapons, the couple mutually [attacked]; / and two such corpses fell there on the bank of the lake.
Then those two, the lotus-eyed man and woman, shone, / and the two corpses were of the very same appearance, O fortunate one.
Resembling the form of a god, father, just like the man, so was the corpse; / whatever was the form of that [woman], just such [a corpse] was seen there.
And just as was the form of the wife, so was the second corpse. / Then, cutting off with a weapon the flesh of the female corpse,
she eats its flesh drenched in blood; / and the man, utterly distressed, likewise eats the flesh of the corpse.
Afflicted by hunger, both eat their flesh; / as long as they had not reached satisfaction, so long was the flesh devoured.
Then, having drunk water from the lake, they became happy, O father; / having stayed there for some time, they departed again by aerial chariot.
Two other women, father, were indeed seen there by me, / endowed with beauty and good fortune, those two women of auspicious marks.
When the flesh was eaten by the two [first ones] in that great forest, O father, / then those two other [women] burst out laughing with loud cackles.
And those two eat their own flesh constantly; / having performed bathing and other rituals, they look upon that flesh right before me.
Two other women, O fortunate one, possessed of a dreadful appearance, / with terrifying fangs and mouths, very frightening, [came] right there.
Then those two said to them repeatedly: 'Give! Give!' / Thus was seen by me, O father, while staying near the forest.
Having carved it out daily, the two indeed eat the flesh; / and the two bodies of the corpses become fully restored again.
Daily descending thus, they and the others as well, O father, / perform the same behavior previously described, while I watch.
This wonder was seen then by me, O father. / You asked, father, and a wonder indeed was seen.
The cause of all this doubt has been recounted before you. / By your grace and with a pleasing mind, explain it!
He who arrived by the aerial chariot together with the woman, O best of the twice-born, / who possessed a divine form—who was that lotus-eyed one?
Who is the woman, O fortunate one, who eats human flesh? / And who is he that came, father, and she too who comes and eats?
Why do those two women laugh then, father? Tell us! / And why did those other two repeatedly say, 'Give! Give!'?
Tell me about those two very terrifying women. / You ought to sever this doubt of mine, father, O you of good vows!"
Having spoken thus, O great king, that bird fell silent. / Having been questioned thus by his third son, Vijvala,
he recounted the entire story while Cyavana also listened.

2.94.m: Kuñjala said: / "Listen, O son, I will explain the whole cause / because of which those two became eaters of their own flesh.
Everywhere, good and bad action is the cause; there is no doubt. / Through meritorious action, son, a person enjoys happiness;
and through action accompanied by sin, they experience misdeed here. / Having thus examined the subtle path with the eye of knowledge of the scriptures,
and having seen the gross dharma and reflected upon it repeatedly, / a person should undertake action with an expert mind.
Just as a sculptor making an image melts the molten metal / with the heat of the fire, son, and with flames on all sides,
and the metal heated gradually by fire becomes liquefied— / whatever kind of molten fluid is poured into the mold, my child,
of that very kind the form is produced, my child; there is no doubt. / Whatever kind of action is done, such is experienced.
Action alone is primary, existing in the form of rainfall; / whatever seed the farmer sows in his fields,
just such fruit does he enjoy, my dear one, without any doubt. / Whatever action is performed, just such is experienced.
Action is the cause of destruction for him; we are all subservient to action. / In this world, action is an heir; action is kinsmen and relatives.
Actions impel a person toward happiness and sorrow here. / Just as gold or silver is cast according to the mould,
so a living being is cast, subject to past action. / These five are seen even while an embodied soul is in the womb:
lifespan, action, wealth, learning, and death. / Just as an artisan makes a lump of clay into whatever he desires,
so action that has been done attaches itself to the doer. / Divinity, or humanity, the state of a beast, or of a bird,
or the state of an animal, or of an inanimate being—a creature attains these by his own actions. / Indeed, he constantly experiences what has been ordained for himself:
sorrow ordained by himself, happiness ordained by himself. / Beginning from the bed of the womb, beings experience the consequences of a past body.
No best of men, whether by force or by wisdom, / is capable of altering action done in a previous body.
They experience only what was done by themselves, both sorrows and pleasures. / Through causes or through reasons, a man is afflicted by his ego.
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows, / so good and bad action follows the doer.
There is no destruction of it except by being experienced; / who is capable of altering past bondage which is action?
Ordained destiny runs after one who is running very swiftly; / it shines through coincidence just as the action done previously.
It stands by him when he stands; it follows him when he walks; / it acts when he acts; it conforms like a shadow.
Just as shadow and sunlight are always closely connected to each other, / so the objects of the senses are afflictions, and old age and the rest are afflictions.
They torment a man afterwards who was already afflicted by previous action. / Wherever a man must experience either sorrow or pleasure,
he is led there forcibly by destiny, as if bound by a rope. / And they say destiny is the bringing about of pleasure and pain for living beings.
Otherwise that action must be reflected upon, whether waking or sleeping. / For otherwise destiny undertakes [its task], and he who wishes to kill is killed;
what is to be protected is well preserved from weapons, fire, poison, and dangerous places. / Just as seeds, trees, shrubs, and even grasses on earth,
even so actions reside in the self and originate there. / Just as a lamp attains extinction from the exhaustion of oil,
so from the exhaustion of action, the body of a living being meets destruction. / Likewise, death from the exhaustion of action is declared by knowers of reality.
Various diseases of living beings and their causes are recorded. / Therefore, action alone is the essential principle for living beings.
The action that was done previously is experienced right here. / What was seen by you and asked about just now, my dear one,
its meaning has been explained by me; those two are indeed experiencing it now. / In the Ānandakānana forest, their very dreadful karma was seen.
I shall explain their conduct; listen, my dear one, as it is told. / This is the realm of action, my dear, while others are realms for enjoyment;
having gone to those, O very wise one, he experiences [the fruits of] creations and the rest. / Sūta said: In the Caula country, there was a king named Subāhu of great wisdom,
handsome, virtuous, steadfast; there was none like him on earth: / a devotee of Viṣṇu, highly intelligent, and very dear to the Vaiṣṇavas.
Meditating upon Madhusūdana with threefold action, / he sacrificed with all sacrifices, such as the horse sacrifice, O king.
And he had a family priest, a brāhmaṇa named Jaimini. / He summoned Subāhu and spoke this word to him:
“O King, make good gifts by which happiness is enjoyed. / Through gifts, a man, having gone to the other world, crosses over difficult realms.
Through giving he attains happiness; he attains eternal fame. / And through giving, matchless renown arises in the mortal realm.
As long as fame remains here, so long does the giver dwell in heaven. / That gift is said to be difficult to make; it is not easily given;
therefore, by every effort, it must always be given by men.” / Subāhu said: “Between giving and asceticism, which is harder to perform,
or which has great fruit in the hereafter? Tell me that, O best of the twice-born.” / Jaimini said: “There is nothing harder on earth than giving.
O King, just one thing is seen visibly, with the world as witness: / Deluded by greed, abandoning their beloved lives for the sake of wealth,
men enter the ocean and likewise the wilderness in this world. / Others resort to servitude, which is established as the dog's life;
and formerly they resorted to agriculture, which abounds in violence and brings much suffering. / The abandonment of wealth, even though acquired with hardship,
and dearer even than life, is very difficult to do, O tiger among men, / especially, O great king, of that which was acquired righteously.
There is no end to what is given with faith according to rule to a worthy recipient. / Faith is the goddess, the daughter of Dharma, purifying and carrying the universe across;
she is Sāvitrī, the mother, and the deliverer across the ocean of worldly existence. / Dharma is accomplished through faith, not by great heaps of wealth;
the sages, though destitute, went to heaven having faith as their dharma. / There are many gifts of various sorts, O best of kings;
there is none superior to the gift of food, which bestows a good destiny on living beings. / Therefore food should be given, accompanied by milk,
and accompanied by sweet and sacred speech. / There is no gift superior to food in this world and in the next,
for delivering, for welfare, and for the sake of obtaining happiness. / Given with faith, according to rule, to a worthy recipient with a pure mind,
a man experiences the fruit of giving even a single meal. / A mouthful from a mouthful should be given, a handful, or a measure—there is no doubt.
The great fruit of that gift becomes imperishable. / And let it not be that a man does not possess even a measure or a handful;
overcoming lack of faith, when a sacred occasion arrives, a man / should feed even a single brāhmaṇa with faith and devotion.
By giving even a single excellent meal of food, O lord of subjects, / having reached another birth, he constantly enjoys food.
Whatever was given in a previous birth with devotion to a worthy recipient once by men, / having attained another birth, he constantly enjoys that very thing.
Those who constantly bestow the gift of food upon brāhmaṇas, / those men, the givers of food, enjoy sweet food and drink.
These sages who have mastered the Vedas declare food alone / to be the life-breath itself, without a doubt, arisen indeed from nectar.
By him indeed were life-breaths given, by whom food was presented. / Therefore, O great king, bestow the gift of food with effort!”
Having heard this from the great-souled Jaimini, the king / asked again that brāhmaṇa Jaimini, who was learned in wisdom.

2.95.m: Subāhu said: / Tell me now the virtues of heaven, O best of the twice-born; / I shall do all this naturally, O foremost of the twice-born.
Jaimini said: / There are charming, celestial, and varied gardens such as Nandana, / sacred, and endowed with all objects of desire;
Beautified all around by trees bearing all desired fruits; / celestial aerial cars frequented by hosts of Apsarases;
Everywhere wondrous, moving at will and obedient, / having the color of the morning sun, adorned with hanging pearls;
Radiant like the orb of the moon, with golden couches and seats, / fully rich in all objects of desire, and free from all sorrows.
Men of meritorious deeds wander among them just as upon earth. / Materialists do not go there, nor do thieves, nor those with uncontrolled senses,
Nor the cruel, nor the slanderous, nor the ungrateful, nor the arrogant. / Men who are truthful, devoted to austerity, heroic, compassionate, intent on forbearance,
Sacrificers, and charitable by nature—those men go there. / There is no disease, nor old age, nor death, nor grief, nor cold, nor heat;
There is no hunger, nor thirst, and no fatigue is found in anyone. / These and many others are the virtues of heaven, O king.
Now listen to the flaws that exist in that very place: / The entire fruit of auspicious action is consumed right there;
And no [new] action is performed there; that is traditionally regarded as the great defect there. / Discontent arises upon seeing the superior, blazing splendor [of others];
And suddenly there comes a fall for those whose minds are filled with pleasure. / The fruit of whatever action is performed here is consumed right there;
This is known as the land of action, O king, while that is considered the land of fruit. / Subāhu said: Great indeed are these defects of heaven related by you;
Speak to me, O twice-born, of those other realms which are flawless and eternal. / Jaimini said: Defects exist indeed up to the realm of Brahmā, O king;
For that very reason, wise men do not desire attainment of heaven. / Above the realm of Brahmā is that supreme abode of Viṣṇu,
The auspicious, eternal Light; the wise know it as the Supreme Brahman. / Fools possessed by sensual desires do not go there;
Those afflicted by deceit, delusion, fear, malice, anger, and greed [do not go there]. / Devoid of possessiveness, free from egotism, beyond duality, with subdued senses,
And devoted to the yoga of meditation, the virtuous indeed go there. / All this has been related to you which you ask of me.
Having thus heard the qualities of heaven, Subāhu, the lord of the earth, / spoke to that high-souled Jaimini, the best among speakers.
Subāhu said: / I shall not go to heaven, nor do I even desire it, O sage; / that action from which a fall is declared, I shall not perform.
O highly fortunate one, I shall certainly never make a gift, / for from gift-giving and longing for its fruit, a man indeed falls.
Having spoken thus, the righteous king of the earth, Subāhu, [thought]: / “Through the yoga of meditation I will worship the lord of the gods, the beloved of Kamalā.”
I shall go to the realm of Viṣṇu, which is free from burning and dissolution. / Jaimini said: You have spoken the truth, O king, which is filled with all supreme good.
Kings devoted to righteousness sacrifice with great sacrifices; / all kinds of gifts are given in sacrifices, O delight of the kings.
First food is given in sacrifices, and garments, betel, / gold, the gift of land, and they bestow the gift of cows.
Through good sacrifices, those best of men go to the realm of Viṣṇu; / kings attain contentment through giving and remain satisfied.
High-souled ascetics always sacrifice in this way: / having begged for good alms, and returned to their own place,
They divide the alms into portions, O king: / one share for a brāhmaṇa, a morsel for a cow, O wise one,
And those rich in austerity give one share to those standing near them; / by the offering of that food, people enjoy the fruit.
Free from hunger and thirst, they indeed go to the realm of Viṣṇu. / Therefore, O king of kings, you too give wealth acquired through righteous means.
From giving, knowledge is obtained; thereafter, through knowledge one attains perfection. / Whichever mortal listens to this sacred, unsurpassable narrative,
He shall attain accomplishment of all aims, and all his sin dissolves; / freed from all sins, he goes to the realm of Viṣṇu.

2.96.m: Subāhu said: / By what kinds of actions do men go to hell after death, / and by what kinds do they go to heaven after death? You ought to tell me that.
Jaimini said: / Those twice-born who, abandoning their sacred brāhmaṇahood, deluded by greed, / subsist on evil deeds—they surely go to hell.
Atheists, violators of bounds, those intent on the realm of lust, / hypocrites, and the ungrateful—they surely go to hell.
Those who, having promised wealth to brāhmaṇas, do not give it, / and men who steal the property of brāhmaṇas go to hell.
Men who are slanderous, arrogant, untruthful, / and speakers of incoherent chatter—they surely go to hell.
Those who steal the property of others, who point out others' faults, / and those who go to other men's wives—they surely go to hell.
Those men who are always engaged in harming the life of living beings, / and those who delight in censuring others—they surely go to hell.
O scorcher of foes, men who breach good wells, tanks, / water-stations, and lakes go to hell.
Those who neglect their wives, children, servants, and guests, / and men whose worship of ancestors and gods has ceased, go to hell.
O king, those who defame asceticism, those who corrupt hermitages, / and those who betray friends—they surely go to hell.
Those who do not contemplate Viṣṇu, the primeval Person, the Ruler, / the Great Lord of all the worlds—they surely go to hell.
Those who spoil fore-sacrifices, sacrifices, maidens, friends, / virtuous people, and spiritual teachers go to hell.
Those who block paths with wood, pegs, / or with desolate stones—they surely go to hell.
Those who mistrust all creatures, who are afflicted by lust, / and who are crooked toward all beings—they surely go to hell.
Those who turn away brāhmaṇas who have arrived for food / and are emaciated by their livelihood—they surely go to hell.
Those men who cause loss of fields, livelihood, houses, affection, / and who shatter hope—they surely go to hell.
Those men who make and sell weapons, / arrow-heads, and bows, O king of kings, go to hell.
Those fools who feel no compassion for an orphan, a distressed, wretched, / disease-afflicted, or elderly person—they surely go to hell.
Those who, having first undertaken vows, later with uncontrolled senses / transgress them due to fickleness—they surely go to hell.
“These people, O king, who go to hell, have been described to you; / now learn from me about those men who are destined for heaven:

Those men who follow dharma through truth, austerity, patience,
giving, and study—they go to heaven.

And those who are devoted to oblations and meditation, dedicated to worshipping the deities,
receiving [little], great-souled—those men go to heaven.

Those who are pure in a pure place, wholly devoted to Vāsudeva,
reciting and singing of Viṣṇu—those men go to heaven.

Those who attentively attend upon their mother and father at all times,
and avoid sleeping during the day—those men go to heaven.

Men who have turned away from all violence, who keep company with the virtuous,
and who are engaged in the welfare of all beings—those men go to heaven.

Men who have turned away from all greed, who endure everything,
and who have become a refuge to all—those men go to heaven.

Men who bestow honour upon their gurus through attendance and austerities,
and who refrain from accepting gifts—those men go to heaven.

Those who serve a thousand guests, and likewise those who give a thousand,
and those who protect thousands—those men go to heaven.

And those who release creatures emaciated by fear,
sin, distress, grief, poverty, and disease—those men go to heaven.

Those who possess their own true nature, and though in their youth, O Bhārata,
are steadfast with conquered senses—those men go to heaven.

Givers of gold, of cows, and of land, O Bhārata,
and of foods and garments—those men go to heaven.

Those who rejoice when asked, give [it], and speak kindly,
and have abandoned desire for the fruit of their gift—those men go to heaven.

Those who produce dwellings, grain, and [necessities] for men
by themselves and give them away, O oppressor of enemies—those men go to heaven.

Those who never speak of the faults even of their enemies,
and who proclaim their virtues—those men go to heaven.

Those who do not torment themselves with jealousy upon seeing the fortune of others,
but rejoice and are glad—those men go to heaven.

Those great-souled ones who practice both in worldly engagement and in renunciation
only what is taught in the Vedas and Śāstras—those men go to heaven.

Those who do not know how to speak an unpleasant word to people,
knowing only pleasing speech—those men go to heaven.

Those who do not make shares [for themselves first] when afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue,
and who offer the food-portion to guests—those men go to heaven.

The makers of step-wells, wells, ponds,
water-booths, houses, and groves—those men go to heaven.

Those who are truthful even among the untruthful, straight even among the crooked,
and benevolent even toward enemies—those men go to heaven.

Born in whatever family, having many sons, living a hundred years,
compassionate, and of good conduct—those men go to heaven.

Those who always make each day fruitful through singular righteousness,
and who constantly observe vows—those men go to heaven.

Those men who look equally upon one reviling and one praising them,
tranquil in mind, having conquered pride—those men go to heaven.

And those who protect brāhmaṇas terrified with fear,
as well as women, or merchant-caravans—those men go to heaven.

Givers of funeral cakes to the ancestors at the Gaṅgā, at the sacred ford of Puṣkara,
and especially at Gayā—those men go to heaven.

Those men who are not in the power of their senses, but established in self-restraint,
having abandoned greed, fear, and anger—those men go to heaven.

Those who protect like children lice, bedbugs, gnats,
and other creatures even as they bite their body—those men go to heaven.
Those who, out of ignorance, hoard according to the prescribed rule, / and people who endure all dualities—those men go to heaven.”

Those who are pure and established in goodness, who do not take delight
in another's wife in action, mind, or speech—those men go to heaven.

Those who do not do blameworthy acts, but perform what is ordained,
knowing their own capacity—those men go to heaven.

Thus all this has been told to you in truth by me, O king:
how a bad destination and a good destination are obtained through actions.

A man who acts adversely toward others goes to a dreadful, exceedingly terrible hell;
for a man who lives always favourably [to others], joy-bringing liberation is stationed not far away.

2.97.m:
Kuñjala said:
Having heard this destination of dharma and adharma spoken by the sage,
the king then addressed that sage.

Let one worship Madhusūdana with oblations and with japa."
Having performed sacrifices and undertaken austerities, that king [went to] the world of Viṣṇu.

Adored with all desired objects, he arrived quickly with joy.
When he had gone to that great world, he did not see the god of gods.
A very acute hunger arose, and an intense thirst began to burn; / and both of these, O greatly wise one, caused immense torment to the soul.
The king too, along with his beloved wife, tormented by hunger and thirst / and beset with immense distress, did not behold Hṛṣīkeśa.
Sūta said: / Thus the king, full of sorrow together with his beloved wife, O best of men, / became utterly bewildered and distraught, exceedingly afflicted by hunger.
The ruler of the earth ran swiftly here and there, / his limbs adorned with every ornament, decked with fine garments and sandalwood paste.
His limbs made radiant by flower garlands, necklaces, earrings, and bracelets, / his body shining with the brilliance of jewels, the king wandered about.
Thus experiencing sorrow even while being praised by panegyrists, / overwhelmed by sorrow and grief, he spoke these words to his beloved:
'I have reached the world of Viṣṇu together with you, O lovely woman, / praised even by sages, mounted upon an aerial chariot, O splendid lady!
By what past action of mine does this fierce hunger increase? / And though I have arrived in Viṣṇu's realm, Madhusūdana is not seen.
What indeed is the cause of this, O fortunate one, that I do not enjoy great fruit? / Or does this sorrow arise from some action of my own?'
Having heard those words of his, she spoke thus to the king.
The wife said: / 'You have spoken the truth, O king; there is no futility in dharma. / The brāhmaṇas who recite the Vedas, the treatises, and the Purāṇas—
shaking off distress and sorrow here, one is freed from all sins / simply by uttering the name of the Lord, Viṣṇu who bears the discus.
Virtuous and exceedingly fortunate people meditate upon Janārdana. / You indeed worshipped the god who holds the conch, discus, and mace;
yet no gift of food or the like was given to the brāhmaṇas as prescribed by the twice-born. / I recognize this as its fruit, that Madhusūdana has not been seen.
Hunger torments me, O king, and thirst parches me dry.' / Kuñjala said: / Being thus addressed by his beloved, the king, his senses troubled with anxiety,
then beheld a highly sacred hermitage that dispels fatigue, / crowded with heavenly trees and beautified by reservoirs,
[It was] filled with stepped wells, reservoirs, and ponds overflowing with holy water, / teeming with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and adorned with white water-lilies.
The hermitage looked splendid, O son, with sages who know the reality, / dense with heavenly trees and graced by herds of deer,
thick with various flowers, filled with delightful fragrances, / crowded with twice-born and perfected beings, and bustling with disciples of sages,
resounding with yogins and lords of yoga, adorned by hosts of gods, / dense with groves of banana trees and decorated with fine fruits,
thronged with diverse trees, endowed with all objects of desire, / always adorned with fine-smelling sandalwood trees and abundant fruits.
It was thus holy, filled with the marks of the absolute. / King Subāhu, then, along with his dearly beloved wife,
entered that most sacred forest that fulfills every wish, / illuminating all quarters, where resided one resembling the sun.
Shining with great, supreme brilliance, resembling the sun, / seated in a yogic posture, wrapped in a yogic band,
Vāmadeva, the best of sages and foremost among Vaiṣṇavas, / was meditating upon Hṛṣīkeśa, who bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
Having seen that great-souled Vāmadeva, the best of sages, / the king went quickly with his beloved wife and bowed down.
Then, seeing the excellent king bowed low, / Vāmadeva greeted the king, accompanied by his beloved, with blessings.
Having seated Subāhu, the best of kings, upon a sacred seat, / he honored him with a seat and other courtesies, with water for washing the feet and the guest-offering.
Honored by the sage, the king, who had arrived with his beloved, / was then questioned [by him], the best of great devotees of the Lord.
Vāmadeva said: / 'I know through divine knowledge, O best of kings, that you are the Cola king, / knower of Viṣṇu's dharma, devoted to Viṣṇu, the best of men.
Have you arrived free from illness, along with your wife of eagle-like eyes?' / The king said: 'I have arrived free from illness, having attained the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
For with supreme devotion, the God of gods, Janārdana, / the Lord of the world, was worshipped by me; pleased with devotion, the Lord of gods—
Why, O revered father, do I not see the god, the lord of Kamalā? / Hunger torments me, O revered father, and an intensely terrible thirst;
from these two we find no peace, nor do we obtain any comfort. / This is the cause of sorrow that has befallen me, O best of sages;
so tell me the cause of it, and out of grace be pleased toward me.' / Vāmadeva said: 'You are indeed always devoted to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O best of kings.
Madhusūdana was worshipped by you with supreme devotion, / with offerings of devotion such as ablutions, and likewise with incense, flowers, and the rest;
yet the Lord of the worlds was not worshipped with food offerings and fruits. / Arriving at the tenth lunar day, O best of kings, you always observed
eating only one single meal, but good food was not given to a brāhmaṇa; / and having arrived at the eleventh lunar day, no food was consumed by you,
yet no food was given to a brāhmaṇa dedicated to Viṣṇu. / Food always exists upon the earth in the form of nectar.
The gift of food in particular was never given by you at any time. / Listen to the herbs and plants, O great king, in their various divisions:
pungent, bitter, astringent, sweet, sour, and saline, / and all the condiments like asafetida in their various forms, O ruler of the earth.
All the plants, the sources of nourishment, were born from nectar. / Having well-prepared that food, combining it with herbs and cooked dishes,

"To the gods who have the form of Viṣṇu"—intending thus, [a gift] is given,
and "to the ancestors who have the form of Viṣṇu", into the hand of a brāhmaṇa.
then, having given to guests, one should feed one's dependents; / and afterward they themselves eat that food resembling nectar.
After death, there is no suffering at all for him, but only happiness, O ruler of the earth. / Brāhmaṇas, ancestors, and gods are in the nature of fields, O king.
Just as a farmer always carries out good cultivation, / so a mortal should carry out cultivation in the field of a brāhmaṇa's mouth, O king.
With the plow of one's natural disposition, one should break the soil using the blade of faith; / the two bullocks are held to be constant intellect and austerity;

The lord who experiences true knowledge, whose self is pure, with water in hand
should dismiss [the brāhmaṇa] in the great field called 'brāhmaṇa' with bows.
Just as a farmer always breaks up the clods of dirt, O king, / engaged in working the field, desiring Viṣṇu, one should propitiate [it];
in the same manner, one should propitiate brāhmaṇas with auspicious, holy words. / The occasion of festivals and holy pilgrimage places is like a cloud for raining:
the field-owner wishing to sow then sows in the field. / In the same way, O king, gifts are given to a pleased brāhmaṇa.
Just as the owner of the field enjoys the fruit / of the field wherein seed has been sown, O great king, so also does the donor enjoy;
both in the hereafter and right here, he becomes constantly satisfied—not otherwise. / Brāhmaṇas, ancestors, and gods are the forms of fields, without a doubt.
Sown for the sake of mortals, O great king, they yield [their fruit]; / the fruit is just like that, of this there is no doubt: as one sows, so one surely reaps.
For sweet fruit does not arise from bitter, O king, / nor, likewise, does bitter arise from that which is called sweet.'

Just as the seed one sows, so is the fruit one enjoys;
he who does not sow a field does not enjoy its fruit.

Likewise, the brāhmaṇas, the gods, and the ancestors have the nature of a field;
they show the fruit even of what has been given, O king, of this there is no doubt.

Whatever action was performed by you, auspicious or inauspicious,
enjoy such [fruit], O king; it cannot happen otherwise.

Never in the past was sweet food or drink
given with a pure mind to gods, brāhmaṇas, or ancestors.

Plentiful, delicious, sweet food to be chewed, sucked, drunk,
and eaten was enjoyed by you yourself; to whom did you ever give [anything]?

Your own body was nourished by you with foods like nectar;
because that was done, O great king, therefore hunger arises [now].

Action alone, O king, is the cause of men's pleasure and pain,
and of birth and death, O fortunate one; enjoy the fruit of that action.

Even ancient great-souled ones reached heaven through their own action,
and went back to the earthly realm when the time came for the exhaustion of their action.

Nala, Bhagīratha, Viśvāmitra, and Yudhiṣṭhira
reached heaven only through action, O king, at their proper time.

Destiny is indeed previous action; through it one obtains pain and pleasure;
who, O king, even an almighty lord, is capable of transgressing that?

Now therefore, O best of kings, even though you have gone to heaven, there arose for you
the violent onset of hunger and thirst; for your action was corrupt.

If a remedy for your hunger is desired by you, O best of kings,
then go and eat your own body remaining in the forest of Ānandāraṇya.

And this great queen of yours appears exceedingly emaciated by hunger."
Subāhu said: "For how long must this deed be done together with my beloved?

Tell me that, O fortunate one: when will favour be seen?
By the giving of what substance is there what merit, O best of sages?

Tell that, O very wise one, if you are pleased now."
Vāmadeva said: "From the gift of food comes great happiness, and from water, O highly intelligent one.

Mortals enjoy heaven indeed, and are not afflicted by sins,
only when a gift has been given by human beings.

Even when the time of death has arrived, all give gifts;
first of all food should be given, accompanied by water.

He should give a good parasol and shoes, and an attractive water pot,
land, fine gold, and a cow—whoever gives these eight gifts,

in heaven the arising of hunger, thirst, and the like does not happen to him;
he is not tormented by hunger, O king, satisfied from the gift of food.

Severe thirst does not arise for him; he is always satisfied.
By the gift of sandals and by the gift of a parasol, O lord of the earth,

the giver obtains shade and a vehicle, O best of kings;
by the gift of shoes... another [result] I declare thus:

from the gift of land, O fortunate one, one obtains all desires;
by the gift of a cow, O great king, one is always nourished with tastes.

Enjoying all pleasures, a man dwells in the world of heaven;
the giver becomes satisfied indeed by the gift of a cow, there is no doubt.

Free from disease, endowed with happiness, contented, and possessed of wealth,
by gold one becomes of fair complexion; of this there is no doubt.

A man becomes glorious, handsome, generous, and an enjoyer of jewels.
When the time of death has arrived, if one gives a gift of sesame,

becoming master of all enjoyments, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus, through exceptional gifts, supreme happiness is attained.

The gift of a cow, the gift of land, and food and water
were never given to a brāhmaṇa by you while living, O king of kings,

nor given even at the time of death; therefore hunger arises.
This cause, arisen subject to the power of action, has been told to you.

For just as an action has been done, so it is experienced.
Subāhu said:
How will my hunger go to cessation, O best of sages?

Dried up by it, my body is exceedingly tormented.
Declare to the two of us an expiation for hunger, O best of the twice-born,

so that there may be peace for me from this terrible deed.
Vāmadeva said:
There is no expiation apart from experiencing [the fruits], O best of kings.

You yourself, being sound, will experience all the fruit of this deed.
Where your body has fallen, and that of your beloved, O lord of the earth,

you two must indeed go from here, without a doubt;
and both of you must consume that very imperishable body,

each your own, O king, without doubt, you together with your beloved.
The king said:
For how long must it be consumed in this way by me together with my beloved?

when you hear it, holy, then you will attain liberation.
All this has been told to you; go, O king, and consume it."

Having heard thus, the king, together with his wife once again,
eats the flesh of his own body along with his beloved.

Daily in this way, O greatly wise one, the body becomes whole just as before;
daily the king eats it, and his queen, O son.

And just as the king eats his body,
the two women constantly laugh; I shall tell their disposition.

Prajñā, the greatly virtuous, together with [Śraddhā, looks at] that king’s conduct;
his unfailing faith indeed constantly laughs.

Prompted by understanding, food dedicated to a Vaiṣṇava,
well resolved upon, was not given to brāhmaṇas with faith.

Thus he eats the flesh of his own body every day,
and the woman also [eats] her own body, which has tastes resembling nectar.

Then, at the end of a hundred years, remembering the great sage Vāmadeva,
he reviled himself, O one of good vows:

"Food was never given by me to the ancestors, to the gods, to the brāhmaṇas;
it was not given to guests, and especially to the aged;

nor was it given out of compassion to the poor and the afflicted."
Thus he eats his own flesh, reviling his own action.

Seeing Subāhu eating his own flesh together with his beloved in this way,
the two women, Prajñā and Śraddhā, laughed then.

At that ripening of his action, the pure-souled one laughs, O king:
"In the context of association with me, it was not given, O evil-minded one."

And Prajñā, with those words, mocks the king again:
"Where has that great delusion gone, by which you were deluded, O king?

By greed joined with delusion one is thrown into the pit of darkness;
falling there, [he says,] 'Cast into a snare of grief, alas!'

Abandoning the path of giving, you went along the path of greed, O king;
consume along with your wife, overcome intensely by hunger!"

Thus Prajñā laughs at him, Subāhu, accompanied by his beloved.
This was indeed the entire reason for the laughter of the two, O son.

While the body of the grieving king was being eaten then,
they two said, "Give, give!"—he was constantly begged.

Hunger and Thirst, O greatly wise one, fearsome in form, terrifying,
begged the lord of kings for food mixed with milk.

All this has been recounted to you, which was asked by you.
What else shall I declare to you? Speak that, O greatly wise one!

Vijvala said:
Recite to me that hymn named Vāsudeva, O father,
by which the king may go to liberation, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

2.98.m:
Sūta said:
When these auspicious words were spoken by the great-souled Vijvala,
Kuñjala, the best of speakers, uttered the sacred hymn.

Having meditated on and bowed to Hṛṣīkeśa, the destroyer of all afflictions,
the giver of all blessings, the hymn to Hari was uttered.

That hymn named after Vāsudeva gives all blessings;
it is the gateway to liberation, joined with joy, giving peace, and increasing nourishment;

it gives all desires, grants knowledge, and increases knowledge—
that hymn of Vāsudeva which was revealed to Vijvala,

named after Vāsudeva, immeasurable, increasing merit.
Having understood all that from his father, Vijvala, the best of birds,

began to go there, having questioned his father then, O king.
To Vijvala, who had resolved to go thus and was a master of knowledge,
the righteous-minded one spoke to his son who was prepared to render aid.

Kuñjala said:
O son, I know that great sin of the king, listen:
go and recite there while Subāhu listens.

The more he hears the supreme hymn, the more he will become full of knowledge;
by the grace of glorious Vāsudeva, indeed, there is no doubt that what I have said will be very auspicious."

Having taken leave of the teacher, flying up with swift strides,
Vijvala then reached the sacred Ānandakānana.

Resorting to the shade of a tree, he sat filled with joy,
having looked out for that king who had come again by aerial chariot.

"When will this king Subāhu come along with his beloved?
At some point I shall release him from his sin by means of this hymn."

Meanwhile, the aerial chariot arrived, adorned with a network of tiny bells,
filled with the ringing of bells, accompanied by lutes and flutes.
resounding with the songs of Gandharvas, accompanied by Apsarases, / abundant in all desires, yet entirely devoid of food and water.
Seated in that chariot, King Subāhu, along with his beloved— / along with his beloved Tārkṣyā—stepped down from the aerial vehicle.
Just as he took up a sharp weapon and began to cut that corpse, / right then a call was made by Vijvala:
"O tiger among men! You who resemble a god! / You commit this merciless act, which even cruel men cannot bring themselves
to do, O tiger among men! What reversal of destiny is this? / A sinful, rash deed, ever censured in the worlds—
why have you undertaken it here, devoid of Vedic conduct? / Tell me truthfully all the reason for this."
Having heard the speech thus uttered by that noble Vijvala, / the great king spoke these words to his beloved:
"O beloved, for a hundred years this has been eaten by me, an evildoer, / yet never has anyone spoken as this one speaks.
While I was thus afflicted by hunger, O beloved, / [that torment] has left my heart, and peace now arises in my mind, O lovely one!
“As long as his speech, which pacifies all sorrow, is heard, / so long does delight abide in my heart, O sweet-smiling one!”
Who is this? A god, a Gandharva, or could he be the thousand-eyed [Indra]? / May the word of the sages come true, which was spoken by the sage long ago!"
Having heard the words thus spoken by her beloved, his beloved, / the wife wholly devoted to her husband, then answered the king:
"What you have spoken is true, my lord; this is a supreme wonder! / Just as it is in your heart, beloved, so it is in my mind as well.
Who is this, bearing the form of a bird, who inquires like a well-wisher?" / Hearing this spoken by his beloved, the lord of the earth,
folding his hands in reverence, said to the bird: / Subāhu said: "Welcome to you, O bird-formed lord of great wisdom!
With my head, together with my wife, / I bow to your two lotus feet; may merit be ours by your grace!
Who are you, speaking such pious words in the form of a bird? / Whatever deed was done in a previous body, O best of beings,
good or evil, its fruit is reaped right here." / Then he recounted his own story before him,
just as had been heard previously when told by his father, Kuñjala: / "Tell me your own tale: who are you that speak to me?"
The excellent bird then spoke these words in reply to Subāhu: / Vijvala said: "Born among the parrots, my father is named Kuñjala;
I am named Vijvala, the third among his sons. / I am no god, nor a Gandharva, nor a Siddha, O mighty-armed one!
I constantly behold such terrible deeds [done by you]. / For how long will you perform such great, violent deeds,
O great king? Tell me that now." / Subāhu said: "The hymn named Vāsudeva, which was spoken of formerly by brāhmaṇas—
when I hear it, O noble one, then I shall attain my proper state. / Indeed, so it was spoken by the pure-souled, self-controlled sage:
'Then I shall be freed from sin, without doubt.'" / Vijvala said: "For your sake I questioned my father, and what he told me,

that eternal truth I shall tell you today; listen, O best of men!"

—Of this hymn named Vāsudeva, Nārada is the ṛṣi, the metre is anuṣṭubh,

[the praṇava] is the deity, and the application in repetition is for the destruction of all sins and the attainment of the four aims of life.
Purifying, supreme, meritorious, knowing the Veda, the abode of the Veda, / the support of knowledge, the support of existence—to the Praṇava, indeed, I bow.
Dwelling nowhere, formless, brilliantly luminous, of great elevation, / devoid of qualities yet bound to qualities—I bow to the supreme Praṇava.
Supremely beloved, of great energy, destroyer of great delusion, / pervading the entire universe, transcendent of qualities—to it I bow.
Who shines everywhere, having become the augmenter of the prosperity of beings, / fearless, connected with mendicants—to the auspicious Praṇava I bow.
Singing the Gāyatrī and the Sāman, the chant itself, lover of song, auspicious, / enjoyer of the songs of Gandharvas—to the Praṇava I bow low.
Reflection itself, the form of the Veda, present in the sacrifice, loving toward devotees, / the source of all the world—to the syllable Oṃ I bow low.
The deliverer of all beings, shining in the form of a boat / for those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence—to the Praṇava, Hari, I bow.
Dwelling in all worlds in a single form and manifold forms, / the abode having the nature of sole liberation—to the auspicious Praṇava I bow.
Subtle, subtler than the subtle, pure, devoid of qualities, the ruler of qualities, / free from material states, the seat of the Veda—to it I bow.
Ever free from unions and separations of gods and Daityas, through contentment, / to be meditated upon by deities and yogins—to that syllable Oṃ I bow.
All-pervading, knower of the universe, supreme wisdom, auspicious, / benevolent, possessing auspicious qualities, tranquil—to the Praṇava, the Lord, I pay homage.
Into whose māyā entered the gods and asuras headed by Brahmā, / yet do not find the supreme, pure gate of liberation—to it I bow.
To the root of bliss, whose intellect is pure, to the pure Haṃsa, higher than the high and lower than the low, / homage be to that leader of hosts, to glorious Vāsudeva of vast radiance!
Shining with the glorious Pāñcajanya and with the Sudarśana bright as the sun, / resplendent with club and lotus—to that Lord I take refuge forever.
Whom the Vedas keep secret, qualified, the support of all qualities / and of the moving and unmoving, possessing splendour equal to sun and fire—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
The treasure that ends hunger, stainless, beautiful in form, resplendent with measured bliss, / reaching whom the worlds of the gods and others live—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
Who ever destroys masses of darkness with his rays, the cause of creation, / radiant with splendour bright as the sun—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
Who shines everywhere with the splendours of the sun, who dries up and gives sap, / who, as wind, moves inside living beings—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
The god who, according to his own will, ever sustains all worlds and rulers of earth, / and who acts like a boat for crossing over—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
Gone within, identical with the world, he ever digests [food] for the stationary and the moving; / having the Svāhā-offering as mouth, the cause of the host of gods—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
Who, gentle and granting virtues, nourishes food in the world / with all meritorious saps and spotless splendour—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
He who is everywhere, the cause of destruction, the refuge of all, composed of all, being everything, / who enjoys sense objects without sense organs—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
Who in the form of the soul sustains the worlds, and from it all moving and unmoving embodied beings, / absolute, composed of knowledge, entirely pure—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.

I seek refuge in that Vāsudeva, the destroyer of the Daityas, the root cause of the destruction of suffering, / who is peaceful, supreme, full of power, vast, and reaching whom the gods attain humility.

I seek refuge in that Vāsudeva, who is happiness, the culmination of happiness, bestower of happiness, lord of the gods, / an ocean of knowledge, lord of the sages, ruler of the immortals, who abides in truth and is endowed with the quality of truth.
