I seek refuge in that Vāsudeva, whose form is the sacrifice's limbs, whose form is the supreme reality, who is joined with Māyā, lord of Lakṣmī, intensely auspicious, / the sole consciousness, the abode of the worlds.
His bed lies in the midst of the ocean, his bed rests on the vast coils of the serpent's body; / I bow down constantly to the pair of auspicious lotus feet of that very Vāsudeva.
Those lotus feet of his, endowed with merit, conferring peace constantly, / attended upon by numerous sacred places, of glorious Vāsudeva, destroy all sin.
I bow down constantly to the lotus foot of glorious Vāsudeva, / shining like a great red water lily, adorned with ankle-bells and rings, which conquers the marks of the lotus.
Ever praised with deep devotion by the gods, accomplished beings, sages, and lords of serpents, / I bow down constantly to that holy lotus foot of glorious Vāsudeva.
I seek refuge in that Vāsudeva, dipping in whose foot-water they go to heaven, purified and free from taint, / and the deeply contented sages attain liberation.
Wherever the water of Viṣṇu's feet is present, there all the sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā, ever reside; / whoever drink it, even if having sinful bodies, go pure to Murāri's lovely home.
Sprinkled with the water from his feet, even those whose bodies are smeared with grave sins / go to the liberation of the Supreme Lord; I bow down constantly to his feet alone.
By the mere eating of the food-offering of that great-souled one who bears the discus, / men obtain the fruit of the glorious Vājapeya sacrifice and become endowed with all their aims.
I seek refuge in that Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of hell and misery, / devoid of illusion, complete, knower of virtues, meditating upon whom people attain a good destiny.

He who is worthy of praise by sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas, and ever worshipped by the gods, / who is the cause of the creation of the universe, the lord of Brahmā and other gods, / who is affectionate, the rescuer of one fallen into the great ocean of worldly existence—to his two pure, supreme, purifying feet I bow with devotion.

Glorious Vāmana who was seen in the sacrificial pavilion by the hosts of gods, a chanter of the Sāma hymns, / who delighted the hosts of gods with the chanting of the Sāma, the sole ruler of the three worlds, / who cleansed Bali of sin through the auspicious glances of his eyes—I praise his supreme, purifying pair of lotus feet.

I praise the lord Vāmana, shining in the assembly of the twice-born at the start of the sacrifice, adorned with the glory of sacred knowledge, / radiant with divine luster, full of grace, resembling a sapphire, / who, wishing the good of the gods, begged the fair son of Virocana: “Let three steps be given to me!”

To behold him, the sages ascended to the solar disc in heaven; / he who then indeed covered the space between moon and sun with his stride— / the hosts of gods instantly merged into the body of him, the holder of the discus, the revealer of the universe; I praise the incomparable stride of that Lord.

2.99.m: Viṣṇu said: / Having heard the purifying hymn, supreme, ancient, destroying sins, full of merit, auspicious, / blessed, a noble sacred song, most worthy of recitation, the king became happy.
His thirst departed, along with hunger; the ruler of the earth became like a god, / and his wife also shone with beauties; both attained the severance of the bonds of sin.

Surrounded by the gods, by the twice-born, and by accomplished beings endowed with devotion to Hari, / that deity, holding the glorious conch, discus, lotus, mace, and sword, approached the taintless king.
Glorious Nārada, Bhārgava, and the virtuous Vyāsa, along with the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, arrived there; / the sage named Vālmīki, devoted to Viṣṇu, arrived, and Vasiṣṭha the son of Brahmā;
the great-souled Garga, endowed with devotion to Hari, Jābāli, Raibhya, and Kaśyapa— / these, dear to Viṣṇu, the foremost of the devotees of the Lord, arrived together with Hari.
Those holy, most fortunate ones, free from stain, devoted to the auspicious lotus feet of Hari, / stood surrounding glorious Vāsudeva, praising the king in various ways.
All the gods, with Agni at their head, Brahmā, Hari, and also the heavenly goddesses, / as well as the kings of the Gandharvas and other fine singers, sang divine, sweet, enchanting songs.

With most sacred hymns filled with Vedic knowledge and conforming to the supreme reality, the sages offered praise. / Seeing the sovereign, the ruler of the earth, the god Hari spoke an enchanting word:
“Choose a boon as you wish, O king; I grant it to you, for I am well-pleased.” / Hearing Hari's word and seeing Murāri speaking before him,
the Lord, dark as a blue lotus, the slayer of Mura, bearing the conch, discus, sword, and mace, / accompanied by Śrī, the supreme Lord, radiant with jewels, adorned with bracelets and garlands,

bright as the sun, well served by the multitudes of gods, well adorned with costly necklaces and ornaments, / with divine fragrances and excellent ointments—with devotional disposition the king bowed to the ground before Hari.
Then, bowing like a stick repeatedly with the word “Victory!”, the great king [said]: / “I am your servant, your attendant standing before you; I know neither devotion nor supreme contemplation.

I have come here with my wife, O Hari; protect me who have taken refuge in you! / Fortunate indeed are those twice-born and mortal men, O Mādhava, whose minds are constantly absorbed in meditation on you,
who, chanting 'O Śiva, O Mādhava,' depart completely pure from here to Vaikuṇṭha. / And those who carry upon their heads the holy water that issued from your lotus feet,
bathed in the water that springs from all the sacred places, those mortals go to the splendid abode of Hari.
I have no yoga, I have no devotion, I have no knowledge, I have no rituals; / through association with whose merit do you grant me a boon?”
Hari said: / “The recitation of the name of Vāsudeva, which destroys great sins, / was heard by you from the virtuous Vijvala, O king, making you free from taint.
Because of that, you have become a partaker of liberation; of this there is no doubt. / Enjoy divine pleasures according with your heart's desire in my realm!”
The king said: / “If indeed a boon is to be given by you to me, a wretched man, O god, / give the foremost excellent boon to Vijvala first.”
Hari said: / “Vijvala's father is the virtuous Kuñjala, adorned with knowledge; / he recites the great hymn to Vāsudeva every day, O ruler of the earth.
Together with his beloved wife and his sons, he shall go to my abode; / and to the one who recites this hymn, I shall always grant the fruit.”
When these auspicious words were spoken, the king said to Keśava: / “Make this most holy hymn fruitful, O Keśava!”

Hari said:
In the Kṛta age, O great king, when human beings praise [me with this hymn],
they attain liberation that very moment; of this there is no doubt.

In the Tretā age in merely a month, but in the Dvāpara age in six months;
and in the Kali age, the mortals who recite it for a single year,

go to the realm of Viṣṇu, O king of kings, which grants liberation.
If a brāhmaṇa, having bathed, recites it at the three junctures of the day or at a single time,

whatever desire he wishes for, that very thing shall become his.
A kṣatriya attains victory, adorned with wealth and grain;

a vaiśya becomes prosperous, and a śūdra becomes happy.
He who recites it to an outcaste will be freed from sin;

the listener never sees dreadful hell at all.
And by the grace of my hymn he will attain all accomplishments.

And he who recites it at the time of a śrāddha while brāhmaṇas are being fed—
his ancestors, satisfied, will go to the world of Viṣṇu, O lord of the earth.

Whether a brāhmaṇa or a kṣatriya recites it at the end of a libation,
his ancestors drink nectar, their minds gladdened.

When a man recites it with devotion during oblations and in the midst of a sacrifice,
no obstacles arise there, and every accomplishment will be attained.

In a dangerous, inaccessible place, in peril from ferocious tigers,
or when facing danger from thieves, he should utter that hymn there.

Peace will surely arise there, O great king, there is no doubt.
When a man approaches the king's gate or in other grand enterprises,

a man should recite ten thousand [repetitions] of the [hymn] named after Vāsudeva,
observing celibacy, properly bathed, and free from anger and greed.

Having worshipped Vāsudeva with a restrained mind, he should offer a tenth part [in] homa
with sesame and grains of rice mixed with clarified butter.

Mortals should then offer an oblation with meditation for each verse.
I never leave the side of such people, always serving them like a good servant.

When the Kali age has arrived, he will attain servitude through this hymn.
It should not be given to just anyone because of the risk of violating the Veda;

he will surely have all his desires abundantly fulfilled.
Listen, O king, to how this hymn was made fruitful by me.

It was created by Brahmā; it was formerly recited by Rudra.
Indra was freed from the murder of a brāhmaṇa and released from sin.

The gods and the ṛṣis, Guhyakas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and immortals,
and the Nāgas who worshipped this hymn obtained their desired attainment.

He will be meritorious, fortunate, generous, and endowed with sons,
who recites my hymn; there is no deliberation needed here.

Come with your wife to my abode, O best of kings!"
A supporting hand was offered by Hari to that lord of the earth.

Kettledrums sounded there, the Gandharvas sang delightfully,
the best of Apsarases danced, and they showered flowers.

The gods and all the ṛṣis praised them with Vedic hymns.
Then, accompanied by his beloved, the king went to Hari.

Rejoicing in his heart, Vijvala sees him being praised by the hosts of gods and Siddhas,
and having arrived in haste, the glorious [bird] stays where his father and mother are.

2.100.m:
Viṣṇu said:
On the charming bank of the Narmadā, under a banyan tree, the father truly dwells.
Vijvala, having arrived, bowed down to his father.

The highly intelligent and virtuous [bird] related the majesty
of the hymn named after Vāsudeva before his father,

and how Viṣṇu had arrived and granted him an auspicious boon;
he related all that with a very joyful heart.

Kuñjala too, having heard the king’s account,
filled with great joy, embraced his son Vijvala,

and said, "A meritorious deed was done by you, my child, for the great-souled king—
a very auspicious benefit, through the glorification of Vāsudeva!"

Having spoken thus to his son, greeting him with blessings,
and repeatedly praising his son who was accompanied by the god,

he remained on the charming bank of the river, while Cyavana looked on.
All this has been told to you: the conduct of those great-souled

Vaiṣṇavas, O great king. What else shall I tell you?
Vena said:
Nectar was presented to me in a conch vessel for drinking.

Hence, what mortal on earth would not have faith to drink it?
Knowledge of Viṣṇu is supreme among drinks in this world at all times.

As this is told by you, there is no satiety in drinking it;
indeed, O lord of the gods, my faith in hearing grows.

By your favor, tell me also of Kuñjala's deeds,
and what that great soul said to his fourth son;

kindly tell me the truth in great detail.
The holy Lord said:
Listen, I shall relate the life of Kuñjala,

and the life of Cyavana, which is endowed with much welfare.
This sacred narrative, O best of men, destroys sin.
A man who hears it with devotion obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

2.101.m:
Sūta said:
The lord of gods, Hṛṣīkeśa, recounted to the son of Aṅga, the best of kings,
the great, auspicious narrative that destroys sin:

"Listen, I will tell the story that bestows welfare,
and the account of the twice-born, the great-souled Kuñjala."

Viṣṇu said:
Kuñjala, the righteous, called his fourth son,
and filled with joy, spoke thus to Kapiñjala:

"What unprecedented thing have you seen, my son? Tell me.
Whither did you go from here to eat, O best of sons?

Declare that, O fortunate one, if you saw anything that bestows great merit.
Kapiñjala said:
What was asked by you, father, that unprecedented thing I shall relate.

What was not seen or heard by anyone, and whence it was never heard by me—
that I will tell right here; listen now, father.

Let all my brothers listen; mother, listen now!
Mount Kailāsa is the best of mountains, white like the moon,

abounding in various minerals, adorned with diverse trees,
and washed on every side with the auspicious and sacred waters of the Gaṅgā, father.

Thousands of diverse, divine rivers,
from which, father, diverse streams have arisen,

and thousands of ponds filled with water are on that great mountain;
there are wide rivers frequented by swans and sārāsa cranes.

On that best of peaks, giving merit and destroying sin,
there are diverse blooming and fruiting forests,

furnished with diverse trees, green and auspicious,
endowed with hordes of Kinnaras and crowded with Apsarases,

splendidly adorned by Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Siddhas, and hosts of gods,
provided with groves of celestial trees and filled with divine states,

rich in beauty with divine fragrances, endowed with diverse gems,
and very beautiful with rocks of white crystal,

made of the brilliance of the sun, O king, filled with radiant lights,
with lovely-scented sandalwoods and with bakula trees having dark flowers.
Adorned everywhere with trees laden with various blossoms, / it is made sweet with the melodious sounds of celestial birds.
Made sweet by the humming of bees and the multitude of trees, / that forested mountain shines with the calls of cuckoos.
Crowded with ten million gaṇas, the temple of Śiva is there, / white with radiant beams, holy, a rocky height that is a heap of merit.
With roaring lions, buffaloes, and then elephants, / and resounding everywhere with the trumpetings of the world-elephants,
thronged with diverse beasts, teeming with troops of monkeys, / and filled with reverberating sounds in its caves by the cries of peacocks,
resplendent with caves, plastered cliffs, peaks, and ridges, / endowed with diverse cascades, and glistening with medicinal herbs,
celestial, of divine virtue, holy, crowded with sacred abodes, / frequented by holy folk—a great mountain that is a heap of merit.
The best of mountains, frequented by Pulindas, Bhillas, and Kolas; / with jagged crests and peaks, the king of mountains shines.
With diverse other sacred, auspicious wonders and blessings, / and by the currents of the Gaṅgā's water, it poured forth a mighty sound.
I went there to Kailāsa, the home of Śaṅkara; / there I saw a marvel such as was never before seen or heard.
Listen, father, and I shall tell all that was spoken by me. / From the peak of the mountain king Meru, holy and of immense majesty,
a stream resembling snow, milk, and gold falls to the earth, / of the Gaṅgā, O noble one, adorned with roar and rushing speed.
Reaching the crest of Kailāsa, it expanded there; / ten yojanas in extent, there lies the great lake of the Gaṅgā.
It shines with abundant, holy, and spotless water; / possessing all-around beauty, it is graced by great geese.
With the sacred, divine, and sweet chanting of the Sāman, / the geese warble there; the lake shines with them.
On its bank, upon a rock indeed, O highly intelligent one, / sat a maiden of the snows, her hair loosened, endowed with the wealth of beauty,
possessed of divine form, endowed with virtues, having divine marks, / and adorned with heavenly ornaments, she shines on its bank.
I do not know whether she is the daughter of the king of mountains, or of the great ocean; / or is she the wife of Brahmā, or could she be Svāhā?
Or might she be the fortunate Indrāṇī, or could she be Rohiṇī? / Such abundance of beauty is not seen among young maidens,
nor among any other truly celestial women whatsoever, O father, / such as the manifestation of form, virtue, and character that is seen here.
The apsarases never possess such beauty and signs / as that limb of hers, bewitching the universe, which was seen by me.
Seated on a slab of rock, overcome by sorrow, / without her many kinfolk, the young girl weeps in sweet tones.
Shedding tears, numerous and resembling pearls, / spotless, they fall right into this lake, O highly intelligent one.
Those drops, resembling pearls, fall into the vast water; / from them arise charming, fragrant lotuses.
Lotuses were born from those tears of her eyes, O highly intelligent one; / in the water of the Gaṅgā they float, countless in number.
Fallen, very delightful, carried along by the current / in the midst of the Gaṅgā's stream, frequented by flocks of geese.
Now, the stream of the Bhāgīrathī has issued from that place; / reaching the peak of Kailāsa, a lovely glen called Ratna,
full of water, it extends for two yojanas, / crowded with flocks of geese and filled with water-birds.
There are lotuses of distinct, various colors there, / in the clear stream, O father, resorted to by hosts of sages.
The lotuses that were born from her tears in the morning / float in the Gaṅgā's water, fragrant and large.
They float upon the clear stream filled with water, / among fine geese, resounding with water-birds.
Sūta said: / On that mountain named Ratna, the Great Lord Ratneśvara, / worshiped by gods and daityas, always abides, O father.
There I saw, O father, a certain holy sage, / covered with a burden of matted locks, wearing no clothes, holding a staff,
supportless, taking no food, exceedingly feeble from austerities, / emaciated in body, a mass of bones bound only with skin.
All the limbs of that great-souled one were smeared only with ashes; / he eats dry leaves that have decayed and fallen.
Absorbed in devotion to Śiva, difficult to approach, performing great penance; / taking the fragrant lotuses born from those tears,
bringing them from the water of the Gaṅgā, the highly fortunate one, / skilled in song and dance, worships the god of gods, Ratneśvara.
Standing at the doorway of that enemy of Tripura, he sings and dances; / then coming to the hermitage, the righteous one weeps in sweet tones.
This unprecedented sight was seen by me, O father, best of speakers! / Tell me by your favor, if you know the cause:
Who is that noble woman? Why does she weep, O father? / Why does that divine man worship the god Maheśvara?
Tell me that in detail, the cause of all my doubt. / Thus addressed by his son, the very wise Kuñjala
spoke in detail to Kapiñjala, while the sage was listening.
